channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: The OBR raised its UK growth forecast for 2026 to 1.2% from 1.1% but cut 2027 to 1.0%, and expects inflation to peak at about 3.8% in 2027, with energy prices the biggest near-term risk, around the Chancellor's first Budget.
item.description:
The Independent reports that the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) raised its UK growth forecast for 2026 from 1.1% to 1.2% and cut 2027 to 1.0%, with growth recovering to 1.6% in 2028, 1.8% in 2029 and 1.7% in 2030, citing rising inflation. Cnyes links the inflation outlook to the energy shock from the Iran war, and the Guardian says the UK's early resilience to the war in the Middle East is fizzling out. The Guardian gives the earlier 2027 forecast as 1.5% and the Independent and the BBC give it as 1.6%, so the size of the cut differs by row. The BBC says the OBR sees energy prices as the biggest near-term risk and expects inflation to peak at 3.8% in 2027. Cnyes gives a peak of 3.75% in early 2027, an average of 3.4% for 2027 and 2.1% in 2028 and 2029, returning to 2% by 2030. The Guardian says inflation is expected at 3.5% this year, against 2% forecast in March, and that borrowing is set to fall to around 2% of GDP in the medium term. The Economic Times says Chancellor John Healey's first Budget focused on the cost of living and energy prices. Yahoo reported before the statement that a 3.9% rise in the National Living Wage to about GBP 13.20 an hour from April was expected. The rows do not give the Budget's tax measures, support for energy costs or any measure for construction or manufacturing.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report official forecasts, not outcomes, and the rows differ on the earlier 2027 figure. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, slower expected growth with higher inflation tends to weigh on construction and capital spending, and a higher minimum wage raises labour costs in labour-intensive industries. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, UK construction and manufacturing customers use bonding, sealing and coating materials, so a weaker 2027 outlook and higher costs could lower or delay orders, and the rows give no figures for either sector. Points that may be worth considering include the Budget's measures on housing, energy costs for industry and business rates, the Bank of England's next decision, and UK construction and manufacturing output data.

The Independent | The Guardian | BBC News | Cnyes | The Economic Times | Yahoo!

item.title: The Fed held its rate at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 October in a 10–2 vote, with two members preferring a quarter-point rise, as US inflation rose to 3.7% in September from 3.4% in August.
item.description:
Il Sole 24 Ore, Business Standard, NBC News, Al Jazeera, MarketScreener and LiveMint report that the Federal Reserve kept its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4.00% on 28 October, as expected, in a 10–2 vote. Il Sole 24 Ore says Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Governor Lisa Cook dissented in favour of a quarter-point rise. Business Standard and MarketScreener say the Fed upgraded its assessment of the economy, with MarketScreener saying it now describes a strong pace, and that its statement signals it wants more evidence on how high rates may need to go to bring inflation back to 2%. MarketScreener reads this as a sign of a rise in December. NBC News says inflation rose from 3.4% in August to 3.7% in September, with the cost of crude oil, diesel and gas a major driver. LiveMint says the pause gives the Fed time to assess the effect of the previous rate rise, and Al Jazeera notes the decision came before the US midterm elections. The rows do not give the full statement, the committee's rate projections, the Chair's remarks or the market reaction.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a rate decision with two dissents and a statement that points to possible further rises, not a rate path. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a policy rate held at this level with a rise under discussion keeps financing costs for mortgages, construction projects and equipment purchases high, and energy-driven inflation limits the room to ease. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, construction and manufacturing customers time projects and investment with financing costs in mind, so a longer period of high rates could slow orders for bonding, sealing and coating materials in the US, and the rows give no figures for either. Points that may be worth considering include the December meeting, US inflation data for October, and mortgage and housing-start data.

Il Sole 24 Ore | Business Standard | NBC News | Al Jazeera | MarketScreener | LiveMint

item.title: Canada and the UAE signed a comprehensive economic partnership agreement on 27 October that would remove or reduce UAE tariffs on more than 99% of current Canadian exports, after 47 days of negotiations, with entry into force expected in 2027.
item.description:
Hürriyet Daily News reports that Canada signed a comprehensive economic partnership agreement with the United Arab Emirates on 27 October as Ottawa seeks to diversify trade beyond the United States. Once fully implemented it would reduce or eliminate tariffs on more than 99% of current Canadian exports to the UAE and improve access for pulses and canola, industrial machinery, power generation equipment and aerospace products. It also aims to reduce non-tariff barriers and widen access for goods and services in sectors including forestry, seafood and engineering, and is expected to enter into force in 2027. The Globe and Mail says the deal was one of several trade and infrastructure agreements signed during the visit of the crown prince of Abu Dhabi to Ottawa, and that both countries cite a record negotiating time of 47 days. Wallstreet-online adds that the UAE reaffirmed an investment commitment of CAD 70 billion that was announced last year, and that energy, infrastructure and technology could benefit. The rows do not give trade values, the UAE tariff levels before the deal, rules of origin, the treatment of chemicals, or the ratification steps.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a signed agreement with an entry date in 2027, not trade already flowing. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a trade pact that opens a market to Canadian machinery and equipment makers can raise their export volumes over time, and a diversification away from the US reduces dependence on one buyer. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, machinery, power equipment and aerospace producers are customers for bonding, sealing and coating materials, so export growth in those products could support demand in Canada, and the rows give no figures for materials or chemicals. Points that may be worth considering include the ratification timetable, the tariff schedule for machinery and equipment, and the UAE investment projects in Canada.

Hürriyet Daily News | The Globe and Mail | Wallstreet:online

item.title: The US Department of Commerce imposed anti-dumping and countervailing duties of about 260% on some box semi-trailers from China on 28 October, to last at least five years, after a US International Trade Commission ruling that they were dumped.
item.description:
Chinatimes reports that on 28 October 2026 the US Department of Commerce imposed anti-dumping and countervailing duties of about 260% on some box semi-trailers imported from China. The row says the US International Trade Commission ruled that the trailers were entering the US market through dumping, meaning at extremely low prices that made it hard for US producers to compete, and that the measures will last at least five years. The same row reports that on the same day the Department of Homeland Security added products of the Chinese genomics group BGI and two affiliates to its entity list, which this brief does not cover. This is one source. The row does not give the Chinese producers named, how much of the 260% is each type of duty, the value or volume of trailers imported, the US producers that filed the case, or the response of China.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a trade-defence measure on one vehicle product, with a duty level and a duration. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, duties of this size can end imports of the named products from the named origin and move buying to US producers or other countries. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, trailer and truck-body construction uses bonding, sealing and coating materials, so a shift of trailer supply to US plants or other origins could change where those materials are bought, and the row gives no figures. Points that may be worth considering include the producers and products named in the Commerce order, US trailer import data, and similar cases on other vehicle products.

Chinatimes

item.title: Japan will impose anti-dumping duties of 27.7% to 42.1% on Chinese and 3.6% to 20.1% on Taiwanese nickel-containing cold-rolled stainless steel sheets and strips from 31 October 2026 for five years, the same rates as its provisional duties of July.
item.description:
Commercial Times, Chinatimes and Lianhe Zaobao report that the Japanese government announced anti-dumping duties on nickel-containing cold-rolled stainless steel sheets and strips from mainland China and Taiwan, to apply for five years from 31 October 2026 until 30 October 2031. Chinese products face 27.7% or 42.1% and Taiwanese products 3.6% or 20.1%. Chinatimes says six Taiwanese companies, including Yieh United Steel and Tang Eng Iron Works, face the 3.6% rate and other Taiwanese producers 20.1%. Commercial Times says the rates equal the provisional duties Japan applied in July 2026 and that the government order is to be announced on 30 October. The rows date the announcement 27 October in some outlets and 28 October in others. They do not give trade volumes or values, the Japanese industries that buy the steel, the response of China or Taiwan, or how the duties were calculated.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a trade-defence measure on one steel product, with rates and dates but no trade values. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, such duties raise the landed price of the named products from the named origins and can move buying towards other suppliers, while the provisional duties Japan applied in July may mean that part of the effect has already happened. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, stainless steel sheet is a metal substrate for coating and bonding in manufacturing, so a change in its supply and price could reach Japanese manufacturers that buy it, and the rows name no user industry and give no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the text of the government order, Japanese import data for the product, and any retaliation or similar measures elsewhere.

Commercial Times | Chinatimes | Commercial Times | Lianhe Zaobao

item.title: Thailand's imports of electric passenger cars rose 138% year on year to USD 421 million in September 2026, with nearly 99% from China, while the government considers an excise tax of about 30% on fully imported electric vehicles.
item.description:
The Straits Times reports, citing government data, that Thailand's imports of electric passenger cars rose 138% year on year to USD 421 million in September 2026, with China supplying nearly 99% of the total. For January to September 2026 imports were USD 2.37 billion, of which 96% came from China. The row says the surge highlights the challenge Thailand is trying to address with higher taxes on imported electric vehicles and that the government is now considering an excise tax of about 30% on fully imported electric vehicles as part of a new structure designed to favour domestic manufacturing. This is one source. The row does not give the number of cars, the date or form of the planned tax, whether it replaces existing rates, Thai production or sales volumes, or the names of the makers.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row gives import values and a planned tax under consideration, not unit volumes or a decision. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a tax that favours domestic manufacturing moves value added from fully built imports to local assembly and local parts, and imports can run ahead of such a tax. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, cars assembled in Thailand use bonding, sealing and coating materials bought locally or imported, while fully built imports do not, so a shift towards local assembly could raise demand from Thai plants, and the row gives no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the date and design of the excise tax, unit data for Thai electric car sales and production, and any new assembly plans by Chinese makers.

The Straits Times

item.title: UK vehicle production rose 36.3% year on year to 74,031 units in September 2026 and car output 38.6% to 70,831, the SMMT says, though the rise reflects the disruption from a cyber incident at the UK's largest automotive employer in September 2025.
item.description:
Commercial Times reports figures from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) showing that UK vehicle production reached 74,031 units in September, 36.3% more than a year earlier, the steepest rise since August 2022. UK car production rose 38.6% to 70,831 units, the strongest September for the UK car industry since 2023. The row says the SMMT noted that the year-on-year rise reflects the disruption caused by a cyber incident suffered by the UK's largest automotive employer in the same month of the previous year. This is one source. The row does not state the comparison period for the 38.6%, the level of September 2025, the output lost in the incident, the figures for January to September, the split between domestic and export output, the split by drive type, or an outlook.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row gives one month compared with a month that the SMMT itself says was disrupted. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a large rise from a depressed base says little about the underlying trend, which shows better in a longer period or against a month before the incident. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, UK vehicle plants are customers for bonding, sealing and coating materials used in bodies, glass and interiors, so September output may have supported demand from them compared with a year earlier, and the row gives no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the SMMT's year-to-date figures, the October data, and the split between domestic and export production.

Commercial Times

item.title: President Trump found on 28 October that imports of industrial machinery and robotics threaten US national security but did not immediately impose tariffs, ordering talks with trading partners and a report within 180 days.
item.description:
Yahoo, the Straits Times and Cnyes report that on 28 October President Donald Trump signed a proclamation agreeing with a Commerce Department report that industrial machines and robotics are imported in quantities and in ways that threaten US national security. He directed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer to negotiate with trading partners to address those imports and to report on progress within 180 days. The Straits Times refers to a probe of more than a year and gives industrial stamping and pressing machines and programmable computer-controlled mechanical systems as examples. The rows say the step spares US manufacturers immediate new tariffs and leaves open duties if the talks fall short. Cnyes says supply chains for robots and machinery still face policy uncertainty, and Yahoo says critics warn that new levies on such imports could raise costs and undercut the aim of boosting US manufacturing. The rows do not give a product list, trade values, the countries concerned, possible tariff rates or the legal basis of the finding.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a finding and a negotiating mandate, not a tariff. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, machinery and robots are capital goods, so duties on them would raise the cost of equipment for the factories that buy them, and an open threat can shape ordering decisions before any duty applies. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, factories that buy this equipment are customers for bonding, sealing and coating materials, so delayed or dearer equipment investment could affect the timing of new production lines, and machine builders themselves use such materials, while the rows give no figures. Points that may be worth considering include the product scope and countries named in later documents, the progress report due in 180 days, and the response of the main exporting countries.

Yahoo! | The Straits Times | Cnyes

item.title: Saint-Gobain's third-quarter revenue rose 0.4% to EUR 11.6 billion and comparable growth of 2.5% was below analysts' expectations, with weak new residential construction continuing to slow growth, Wallstreet-online reports.
item.description:
Wallstreet-online reports in a news roundup that the French construction materials group Saint-Gobain continues to feel the weakness of the market for new residential property. The row says the company's third-quarter revenue was EUR 11.6 billion, 0.4% more than a year earlier, and that comparable growth of 2.5% was below the expectations of analysts surveyed by Bloomberg. This is one source and a short roundup. The row does not give the analysts' expectation, the split of revenue by region or by business, the reasons for the gap between 0.4% and 2.5%, such as currency or acquisition effects, the performance of renovation and non-residential building, or the company's outlook.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row gives group revenue growth and an analyst comparison, not volumes by product. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, comparable growth normally leaves out currency and acquisition effects, so a gap between it and reported growth points to such effects, and a materials group's revenue reflects demand from new building and renovation together. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, new residential building uses adhesives, sealants, coatings and other construction chemicals alongside the products such groups sell, so continuing weakness in new housing could limit demand in that segment, while the row gives no figures for chemicals or for adhesives. Points that may be worth considering include the group's regional and business-line figures, the state of renovation demand, and the third-quarter releases of other building materials producers.

Wallstreet:online

item.title: German car production in the first nine months of 2026 was still 15% below the 2019 level and EU car output 17% below its level before Covid, the Neue Zürcher Zeitung writes, adding that employment in the German car industry fell to 690,000.
item.description:
The Neue Zürcher Zeitung writes, in a piece on European industry beyond cars whose web address places it in the opinion section, that car production in Germany in the first nine months of this year was still 15% below the pre-crisis level of 2019. It says more than 40,000 jobs were lost in the German automotive industry in the first half of the year, which brought employment to 690,000, the lowest level in twenty years, and that the number of cars produced in the EU is 17% below its level before the Covid pandemic. The piece adds that stronger competition with China is hurting European industry well beyond cars, because many Chinese products are components such as electronic parts and batteries, and it names VW, Miele, Alstom, Siemens and Stadler Rail among companies that benefit from cheaper parts bought in China. The row is a summary of an article and not a statistical release. It does not name the source of the figures, give the number of cars produced, state the comparison period for the EU figure, or split production by plant location or by drive type.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row combines production, jobs and a view on Chinese competition, with no volumes in vehicles. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a production level well below 2019 means fewer vehicles each year that need materials, while the model mix decides how much material goes into each one. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle bodies, glass, interiors and electronics are bonded, sealed and coated in assembly, so lower output in Germany and the EU could keep demand from automotive customers below earlier levels, and the article's remark on parts bought in China could affect which suppliers are qualified, while the row gives no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the production statistics behind the 15%, the sourcing of electronic parts and batteries, and whether the employment figure moves again in the second half.

Neue Zürcher Zeitung

item.title: China's new-home prices rose 0.1% from August in first-tier cities, were flat in second-tier and fell 0.2% in third-tier cities in September, while Shanghai's existing-home prices turned positive year on year, official data show.
item.description:
China Economic Net reports, citing the National Bureau of Statistics, that in September 2026 new commercial housing prices in first-tier cities rose 0.1% month on month, the same as in August, that second-tier cities moved from a decline to flat, and that third-tier cities fell 0.2%, a decline that did not widen. Among the 70 large and medium-sized cities, the number with a monthly rise in new-home prices increased by two to 17. For second-hand homes, first-tier prices rose 0.2% month on month, 0.1 percentage points more than a month earlier, and the number of cities with a monthly rise grew from three to nine. Shanghai became the first city in this round of adjustment where second-hand prices turned positive year on year. The national unsold area of new commercial housing fell year on year for the seventh month in a row. The rows say the Bureau also released investment and sales data for January to September but do not give those figures. They also give no national average price change, no year-on-year figures for new homes and no reasons for the changes.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows give price changes by city tier, not sales volumes, construction starts or investment. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, prices that stop falling in some tiers do not by themselves show a recovery in new building, because construction depends on sales, unsold stock and developers' funding. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, new housing construction and renovation use bonding, sealing and coating materials, so a market that is stabilising in the larger cities could support demand from Chinese construction customers, while a fall in unsold stock may take time to reach new starts, and the rows give no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the Bureau's January to September sales and investment data, price changes in third-tier cities, and whether more cities report year-on-year gains in existing-home prices.

China Economic Net | China Economic Net
